newsitem.title: SWEDEN: ASSIDOMAN PLANS WEST EUROPEAN ACQUISITION.
newsitem.headline: ASSIDOMAN PLANS WEST EUROPEAN ACQUISITION.

text.p: Swedish forestry company AssiDoman said on Tuesday it was planning this autumn to make an acquisition in Western Europe to add to its packaging division.

"The acquisition we have in the pipeline is in Western Europe and its main line is corrugated cardboard," managing director Lennart Ahlgren told a news conference after releasing the company's six month results.
He said the acquisition would take investments for the year to over eight billion crowns ($998.1 million).
Elsewhere AssiDoman said in the next two to three years it could start up a further three satellite sack factories in Moscow, Perm and Volgograd, initially equipped from its Segezha mill in Karelia.
Production at Segezha had now started up again after a production stop due to a dispute over ownership.
AssiDoman said it intended to cut staff numbers from its current workforce by 900.
"We have identified further need to cut the number of employees," said economic director Christina Liffner, adding that the cuts would be made overseas.
"This will involve costs of some tens of millions of crowns."
She said the company had put aside 270 million crowns to cut 900 staff.
"About 400 have left the company and we estimated that we will have about 200 left at the end of the year. Of the reserves of 270 million crowns about 130 million crowns have now been dispersed."

AssiDoman on Tuesday posted a slightly higher than expected profit after financial items of 859 million crowns against expectations of 819 million crowns. This compared to a profit for the first half of 1996 of 1.23 billion crowns.
Ahlgren said the improving performance is expected to continue.
"The rolling 12 month curve has moved and is continuing up," Ahlgren said.
He said this positive trend was strengthened by the fact that turnover in the second quarter of 1997 was 40 percent better than the same period a year ago.
Alhgren would not forecast a higher profit after financial items this year against 1996.
"The curve is improving but by how much we don't know," he said.
